stories.title: Aerospace and Defense Overtake Tech as L.A.’s Biggest VC Magnet
stories.excerpt: Aerospace and defense have overtaken the traditional tech sector as the top recipients of major venture capital investments in Greater Los Angeles, further fueling demand for industrial and advanced manufacturing space across Southern California. Companies in the overlapping industries have attracted $20.6 billion in funding since 2020, more than double the $10 billion raised by technology companies over the same period, according to a new JLL report on funding rounds of at least $500 million in the L.A., Long Beach and Anaheim metro areas. The shift has accelerated in 2026. Aerospace and defense companies accounted for 72 percent of all major venture funding tracked by JLL so far this year. By comparison, in 2021, tech companies took 74 percent of VC funding. Major venture funding overall has increased 547 percent since its 2023 low, while late-stage rounds accounted for 46 percent of the capital raised. Companies receiving investments through rounds of at least $500 million collectively signed more than 4.8 million square feet of office and industrial leases across the region since 2020. The influx of capital is helping to prop up some of L.A. County’s industrial submarkets even as traditional warehouse demand slows. Aerospace and defense tenants signed more than 400,000 square feet of new leases in the South Bay during the third quarter, keeping Class A industrial vacancy at 4.6 percent, according to JLL. Overall South Bay industrial vacancy stood at 5.3 percent in the third quarter, down from 7.4 percent a year earlier. In the Mid-Cities — the municipalities near the border with Orange County — vacancy declined to 6.3 percent from 7.2 percent annually, while Central L.A. recorded 4.5 percent vacancy, down from 7.1 percent, per JLL data. The momentum contrasts with the broader market, where industrial leasing volume fell approximately 30 percent from the second quarter. stories.summary: Aerospace and defense have surpassed tech as the top venture capital magnet in Greater Los Angeles, attracting $20.6 billion since 2020 compared to $10 billion for tech. This year, 72% of major VC funding (rounds of $500M+) flowed to aerospace/defense versus just 26% to tech. VC-backed companies across both sectors have leased 4.8 million square feet of office and industrial space regionally since 2020.
stories.impact: This funding shift signals sustained demand for industrial and advanced manufacturing space across the L.A., Long Beach, and Anaheim metros. As aerospace/defense companies grow and scale operations, multifamily developers should anticipate sustained in-migration of skilled workers and engineers to Southern California, lifting rental demand and rent growth in submarkets proximate to aerospace clusters (e.g., Long Beach, Santa Ana, Torrance areas). Industrial land values and leasing rates will remain competitive; multifamily developers competing for the same markets should monitor workforce concentration and plan accordingly.

stories.title: KÜHL Will Open First New York City Flagship Store
stories.excerpt: KÜHL, a Utah-based outdoor apparel and lifestyle brand, has signed a multi-year lease for approximately 3,000 square feet of storefront retail space at 520 Fifth Ave., Rabina’s 1,002-foot mixed-use supertall tower at the corner of Fifth Avenue and 43rd Street in Midtown Manhattan. The location will serve as KÜHL’s first New York City flagship and is slated to open in fall 2027. KÜHL was represented by Brandon Miller at Masonre. Rabina was represented by Richard Johnson, Charlie Koniver, Logan Chambers-Powell and Sam Masters at Odyssey Retail. “From the beginning, our vision for 520 Fifth Ave. was to create a true mixed-use destination where each component strengthens the others,” said Josh Rabina, president of Rabina. “KÜHL brings a distinctive brand and a strong point of view to the retail experience, while introducing another reason for New Yorkers and visitors alike to engage with the building beyond its residences, offices, and private members club, Moss.” The post KÜHL Will Open First New York City Flagship Store appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: KÜHL leases 3,000 SF retail at 520 Fifth Ave., Midtown Manhattan

stories.summary: Utah-based outdoor apparel brand KÜHL has signed a multi-year lease for approximately 3,000 square feet of retail space at 520 Fifth Ave. in Midtown Manhattan. The flagship store is slated to open in fall 2027 in Josh Rabina's 1,002-foot mixed-use supertall tower at the corner of Fifth Avenue and 43rd Street. The building combines residential, office, and a private members club.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development demand and supply dynamics. This retail anchor tenant announcement is a positive signal for the building's mixed-use viability and residential leasing momentum (e.g., amenity richness, foot traffic, brand prestige), but does not shift broader Manhattan rental demand or supply pipelines. Developers tracking the supertall market in Midtown should note stabilized retail leasing as a de-risking factor for residential components.

stories.title: South Florida Casino to Rebrand as Margaritaville
stories.excerpt: Fontainebleau Development and Margaritaville on Thursday unveiled plans for a $300 million redevelopment of the Big Easy Casino in Hallandale Beach, Fla., as Margaritaville Casino, set to open in the first half of 2028. The casino last month told the Hallandale Beach Planning and Zoning Board of its plans to develop a new 214,428-square-foot casino with a parking garage at 831 North Federal Highway. The new casino will feature a gaming floor with slot machines and a poker room, plus restaurants, bars and live entertainment, Fontainebleau Development said in a statement. Margaritaville Casino will have “a dedicated sports concept,” the developer said, although the Seminole Tribe of Florida holds exclusive rights to sports gambling in Florida. The project is expected to create 400 permanent jobs. The 24-acre site is home to a repurposed greyhound track that opened in the 1930s. The facility added slot machines in 2004 and opened as the Big Easy Casino in 2018. Jeffrey Soffer, chairman and CEO of Fontainebleau Development, acquired the property in 2018. Despite the involvement of Soffer – who operates the Fontainebleau Las Vegas – the Big Easy ranks dead last in slot machine revenue among South Florida’s eight state-sanctioned casinos. The Big Easy’s slots brought in $38 million in revenue in the 2025-26 fiscal year, a fraction of Magic City’s $148 million, according to the Florida Gaming Commission. stories.impact: This hospitality/gaming anchor investment signals Fontainebleau's confidence in the Hallandale Beach coastal corridor and may drive ancillary residential and hotel demand nearby. South Florida multifamily developers should monitor population and visitor traffic patterns post-opening; a destination casino typically draws regional tourism, convention activity, and may attract relocating hospitality/service workers. The project does not directly compete with or supplant residential development but could elevate the submarket's appeal for Class A multifamily projects near the site.

stories.title: Walker & Dunlop Arranges $270M Refi for Journal Square Apartments
stories.excerpt: Walker & Dunlop, Inc. arranged $270,000,000 in refinancing for The Greyson, a 28-story, 622-unit, Class A mixed-use residential tower developed by Nasser Freres at 25 Cottage St. in Jersey City’s Journal Square neighborhood. The financing marks a significant milestone for the development, supporting its transition from construction to stabilized operations. Walker & Dunlop Capital Markets Institutional Advisory served as exclusive advisor to Nasser Freres, arranging a floating-rate, interest-only bridge loan from affiliates of Apollo. The transaction was arranged by Keith Kurland, Aaron Appel, Adam Schwartz, Jonathan Schwartz, Jordan Casella, Christopher de Raet and Jack Krentzman. “Journal Square has undergone a remarkable transformation, and The Greyson exemplifies the caliber of development attracting investment to the neighborhood,” said Kurland. “With its exceptional location, extensive amenities, and proximity to Manhattan, the property is well-positioned to capitalize on the area’s continued growth. We’re pleased to have worked with Nasser Freres and Apollo to execute this transaction.” The post Walker & Dunlop Arranges $270M Refi for Journal Square Apartments appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.summary: Walker & Dunlop Capital Markets arranged a $270 million floating-rate, interest-only bridge loan from Apollo affiliates for The Greyson, a 28-story, 622-unit Class A mixed-use residential tower in Jersey City's Journal Square neighborhood. The financing supports the development's transition from construction to stabilized operations, marking a refinancing milestone for Nasser Freres.
stories.impact: This refinancing demonstrates capital market appetite for well-located, Class A multifamily in the Jersey City Journal Square submarket, a prime Hudson County redevelopment node. The move from construction to stabilized debt indicates strong lease-up and NOI generation, validating the market's fundamentals. For multifamily developers considering the New Jersey waterfront, this signals that lenders are actively financing quality assets near Manhattan transit (PATH), supporting continued supply and investment momentum in the area; cap rates and financing terms remain competitive for stabilized assets.

stories.title: AI’s Rewards Outweigh Risks for Commercial Real Estate: Forum
stories.excerpt: Watch the full event here. Which areas of commercial real estate are transforming their business thanks to artificial intelligence? The answers might surprise you. Industry leaders discussed the ways they are adopting and adapting to the latest technology revolution Wednesday at Commercial Observer’s latest event, AI & Innovation Forum: Rewriting Real Estate: Transformational Case Studies & a Timely Tech Outlook for 2027. Emceed by CO finance reporter Brian Pascus, the virtual event’s panelists discussed not only the panic of the past week’s nationwide outages — between Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and various banks — but also where they are seeing the best momentum in their business. Clockwise from top left: Guy Vardi, Nikki Greenberg, Rej Singh, and Alon Gorbonos. For Vardi, inspiring confidence in technology, especially considering the outages, isn’t so much a factor compared to awareness that nothing is infallible. “I assume that everything that I’m going to build is going to break, it’s not going to work, it’s not reliable, it’s a very dangerous experiment,” Vardi said. “As a consequence, we structure the team at Silverstein in a quite unique way. stories.title: MMCC Arranges Acquisition Loan for Historic Industrial
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap Capital Corporation (MMCC) arranged $10.2 million in financing for the acquisition of a 1,007,647-square-foot industrial property located at 1 Main St. in Whitinsville, MA. Robert Damigella, managing director in MMCC’s Boston office, secured the loan with a regional bank. The financing features a 10-year term, 75% loan-to-value, a 6.85% interest rate and a 25-year amortization period. Originally built in 1847 as the Whitin Machine Works, the historic property has been reimagined into a commercial hub. Located in downtown Whitinsville, the property offers proximity to major routes including Route 495, the Mass Pike and Route 146, and features several loading docks. “Properties with this much character and history are rare, and our goal was to deliver a financing structure that supports the buyer’s plans for the asset,” said Damigella. “We’re pleased to have closed a competitive loan that does exactly that.” The post MMCC Arranges Acquisition Loan for Historic Industrial appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.title: Bell Partners Spends $149M on MF Property in Issaquah, Washington
stories.excerpt: Atlas Apartments, a 344-unit multifamily community in Issaquah, Washington, was acquired by Bell Partners in a $149-million transaction. The property was sold by Kennedy Wilson, who had owned the asset since 2017. The three-building, five-story multifamily community covers 5.1 acres at 1036 7th Ave. NW in downtown Issaquah. The property features a mix of studio, one- and two-bedroom homes averaging 895 square feet in size. Units amenities include quartz countertops, stainless steel appliances, floor-to-ceiling windows and in-unit laundry. Many units also have views of the Issaquah Alps and the adjoining stream. There are over 28,000 square feet of community amenities, including two fitness studios, co-working pods, resident lounges, a coffee bar, secure bike storage and four landscaped courtyards with outdoor gathering spaces. Atlas is within walking distance of downtown Issaquah’s retail, dining and entertainment offerings. It is also a two-minute drive from the Issaquah Transit Center and within a 30-minute drive to major employers in Bellevue, Seattle and Redmond, as well as many of the region’s largest employment centers. Eli Hanacek, Kyle Yamamoto and Natalie Kasper on CBRE’s Pacific Northwest Multifamily team represented Kennedy Wilson. stories.summary: Bell Partners acquired Atlas Apartments, a 344-unit multifamily community in Issaquah, Washington, for $149 million. The three-building, five-story property spans 5.1 acres in downtown Issaquah and features studio, one-, and two-bedroom units averaging 895 square feet with modern amenities. The asset, sold by Kennedy Wilson, benefits from proximity to major tech employment hubs in Bellevue, Seattle, and Redmond.

Developers planning new multifamily in this submarket should expect persistent demand from Amazon, Microsoft, and other Bellevue/Redmond employers. The sale also suggests capital deployment by institutional buyers seeking lower-velocity, transit-accessible suburban markets; competing developers should monitor cap rate compression and land cost escalation in downtown Issaquah and similar satellite tech markets.

stories.title: Red Apple Group Files Plans for 99-Unit Residential Project at 253 West 24th Street
stories.excerpt: John Catsimatidis’s Red Apple Group has filed plans to build a 99-unit residential building at 253 West 24th Street in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood, according to records with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB). Catsimatidis purchased the 59,250-square-foot building, which sits next to Red Apple’s development site at 280 Eighth Avenue, in 2024 for $22.5 million, Commercial Observer previously reported. If approved, Red Apple plans to construct a 15-story residential property at 253 West 24th Street with 99 units, 17 of which would be affordable units, according to the Thursday filing. It’s unclear whether the development would be part of Catsimatidis’s 280 Eighth Avenue project, which was set to stand 13 stories tall and include 104 rental units, according to New York YIMBY. Chris Fogarty from Fogarty Finger is the registered architect on the West 24th Street project. Catsimatidis and Fogarty did not immediately respond to CO’s requests for comment. The plans for 253 West 24th Street call for between five and seven apartment units across the first through 15th floors. Residents will have access to a variety of amenities including a rooftop terrace, a lounge, coworking spaces, a children’s playroom, bike storage and a gym, according to PincusCo. It is unclear if Red Apple Group landed on 99 units for this property as a way to utilize New York’s 485-x tax abatement program. The often criticized program comes with generous construction wage requirements for buildings with 100 or more units. Properties with 99 units or fewer can still utilize the program without being subject to those wage requirements. Between July 2024 and September 2026, the Real Estate Board of New York (REBNY) found there were 172 proposals for 99-unit buildings in New York City. stories.title: Blue Owl Preps $513M CMBS Data Center Deal
stories.excerpt: The mounting political headwinds confronting data centers are not slowing the sector’s presence in the capital markets. Blue Owl Capital is slated to access the single-asset, single-borrower (SASB) commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) market with a $513 million deal to finance the acquisition of a newly constructed data center in Northern Virginia fully leased to Amazon, Bloomberg reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the transaction. Blue Owl Digital Infrastructure Trust, an affiliate of Blue Owl Capital, acquired the 363,220-square-foot data center for $779.5 million, Commercial Observer previously reported. The SASB loan is securitized by the 54-megawatt Project Crossing III data center project in Gainesville, Va., where Amazon has a long-term lease that runs through 2042 with two five-year renewal options, according to Bloomberg. The property encompasses the third data center in the Gainesville Crossing Data Center campus that will eventually feature five facilities with 326 megawatts. The Gainesville Crossing campus was developed by Corscale Data Centers and Affinius Capital, which secured a $975 million loan from Blue Owl in June to recapitalize the newly built data center, CO reported at the time. The property is in Loudon County, which on Tuesday adopted a 12-month moratorium on new data centers after the area became home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world through large-scale developments over the last decade. News of the CMBS deal was reported hours before Michael Lascher, head of capital markets and asset management at Blue Owl, spoke at New York University Schack Institute of Real Estate Capital Markets conference Wednesday about continued market appetite for the sector despite recent political and community opposition to the projects. stories.summary: Blue Owl Capital is preparing a $513 million single-asset, single-borrower (SASB) CMBS securitization to finance a newly constructed data center in Northern Virginia. The 363,220-square-foot Project Crossing III data center is fully leased to Amazon on a long-term lease through 2042 with two five-year renewal options. This should reinforce rental demand in submarkets near tech corridors (e.g., Ashburn, Dulles area, Leesburg), but competition for land and labor from industrial/data center development may elevate construction costs and reduce developable multifamily sites.
